collections.name: Women's Shawls
collections.heading: Women's Shawls
collections.description: Handwoven shawls for women in pure Pashmina, cashmere and fine Kashmiri wool — from undyed heritage pieces to fully embroidered occasion shawls.
seoContent: A shawl is the most useful thing in an Indian wardrobe and the hardest to buy well. What separates one shawl from another is not the pattern but the fibre and the loom: the micron count of the pashm, whether it was spun on a charkha or by machine, and how many picks per inch the weaver was willing to work at.

Our women’s shawls are made in three weights. Pure Pashmina at around 180 grams for occasion and evening; cashmere at 250–320 grams for daily winter wear; and Kashmiri handloom wool above 400 grams for genuine cold. Every piece is finished by hand and ships with a certificate recording the weaver’s name.

If you are buying your first, start with an undyed piece — the Ivory Heritage or the Warm Beige Ring Pashmina. Undyed cloth hides nothing, so it is the honest way to judge quality, and neutrals outlast every trend.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a shawl and a stole?
faqs.answer: Width. A shawl is roughly 100–110 cm wide and is meant to wrap; a stole is 70 cm or narrower and is meant to hang. Both are typically 200–220 cm long.

faqs.question: Which shawl is warmest?
faqs.answer: Kashmiri handloom wool is the warmest by weight, followed by brushed cashmere. Pure Pashmina is the warmest relative to its weight — it is remarkably light for how much heat it holds.

faqs.question: How should I store a shawl between seasons?
faqs.answer: Folded flat in a breathable cotton or muslin bag, never on a hanger, with a cedar block nearby. Refold along a different line each year so permanent creases do not set.

collections.name: Women's Pashmina
collections.heading: Women's Pure Pashmina
collections.description: Certified pure Pashmina for women — hand-combed Changthangi fibre, charkha-spun and handwoven in Kashmir.
seoContent: Pashmina is not a style of shawl. It is a fibre: the winter underfleece of the Changthangi goat, combed by hand each spring on the Changthang plateau at over 4,000 metres. At 12–15 microns it is roughly half the diameter of fine merino, which is why a Pashmina shawl can weigh under 200 grams and still keep you warm.

Everything in this collection is pure pashm — no blending, no substitution. Each piece is spun on a hand charkha, woven on a wooden handloom and finished by hand, and ships with documentation recording the fibre grade and the weaver.

collections.heading: Men's Shawls
collections.description: Men’s shawls in pure Pashmina and Kashmiri handloom wool, cut long and narrow to hang cleanly from the shoulder.
seoContent: A men’s shawl is cut differently from a women’s: more length, less width, so it falls in two straight columns rather than wrapping. Traditionally it is worn over a bandhgala or kurta, folded once lengthwise and draped over one shoulder.

We make them in two weights. Pure Pashmina for evening and occasion, where lightness matters more than bulk; and Kashmiri handloom wool at 400 grams and above for genuine winter, brushed twice so it softens with wear rather than wearing out.

faqs.question: What length should a men’s shawl be?
faqs.answer: A 110 × 220 cm shawl suits most men. Anything shorter tends to sit awkwardly when folded lengthwise over the shoulder.

faqs.question: Can a men’s shawl be worn with western tailoring?
faqs.answer: Yes — worn as an oversized scarf over an overcoat it works well. For that use, a narrower stole is usually easier to manage.

collections.name: Pure Pashmina
collections.heading: Pure Pashmina
collections.description: Nothing blended, nothing substituted. Hand-combed Changthangi fibre, charkha-spun and handwoven in Kashmir.
seoContent: Most cloth sold as "pashmina" is viscose, or wool with a small percentage of pashm blended in. Pure Pashmina means the yarn is entirely the underfleece of the Changthangi goat, hand-combed rather than shorn, and spun on a charkha rather than a mill frame — machine spinning breaks fibre this fine.

Every piece in this collection carries a GI-registered craft certificate recording micron grade, loom number and the name of the weaver who finished it. If a shawl cannot tell you those four things, it is not pure Pashmina.

bannerImage.alt: Pushmina pure pashmina collection — handcrafted Indian textiles

faqs.question: How can I tell pure Pashmina from a blend?
faqs.answer: Burn test aside, look for irregularity: hand-spun yarn varies slightly in thickness, so the weave is never perfectly uniform. Machine-made "pashmina" is flawless, glossy and cold to the touch. Genuine pashm feels warm immediately and has a matte, slightly hazy surface.

faqs.question: Does the ring test really work?
faqs.answer: For fine shawls, largely yes — cloth woven from sub-14-micron fibre will pass through a wedding ring. It does not work on heavier or embroidered pieces, and a thin viscose scarf will also pass, so use it alongside other checks.

faqs.question: Why is pure Pashmina expensive?
faqs.answer: One goat yields around 150 grams of usable fibre per year, and a shawl needs the yield of three to four goats plus six weeks on a handloom. The cost is almost entirely fibre and labour.

collections.name: Kashmiri Collection
collections.description: Sozni, kani, jamawar and tilla — the four great needle and loom crafts of the Kashmir valley.
seoContent: Kashmir’s textile crafts divide into what is built into the cloth and what is added to it. Kani is woven — the pattern is constructed thread by thread on small wooden bobbins. Sozni, tilla and papier-mâché work are embroidered onto a finished ground.
Kani is the rarer and the slower. A full-field kani shawl can take two weavers close to two years, working from a coded pattern script called a talim that only trained weavers can read.

products.name: Ivory Heritage Pashmina Shawl
products.tagline: The house classic, in undyed Ladakhi Pashmina.
products.description: Our founding piece. Spun from fibre combed from Changthangi goats at 4,500 metres, hand-woven on a wooden handloom over six weeks, and finished with a whisper-fine sozni border in matching ivory thread.
story: The Ivory Heritage is the shawl Pushmina was built on. It begins with raw pashm no thicker than a strand of mist — around 13 microns — combed by hand from the underfleece of Changthangi goats wintering on the Changthang plateau.

Because the fibre is left undyed, nothing hides the weave. Every pick of the weft is visible, which is why this piece is given to our most senior weavers and why no two ever leave the loom quite alike.

products.tagline: Eighteen months of needlework, one shawl.
products.description: A pure Pashmina ground carrying continuous sozni embroidery in a chinar-leaf trail. Worked with a single needle in silk thread so fine that the reverse of the shawl is as clean as the face.
story: Sozni is the slowest of the Kashmiri needle crafts. A master embroiderer covers perhaps a square inch of ground on a good day, which is why a fully worked shawl can occupy one pair of hands for the better part of two years.
The chinar leaf running through this design is the emblem of the Kashmir valley — the same motif you will find carved into the walnut ceilings of Srinagar’s old houses.

posts.title: The Kani Weave, Explained
posts.excerpt: No shuttle, no jacquard, no printing. Dozens of wooden bobbins, a coded script and up to two years on one loom.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: Wooden kani bobbins loaded with coloured yarn on a handloom

blocks.text: Almost every patterned textile you own was printed, or woven on a loom that automates the pattern. Kani does neither. The design is built into the cloth by hand, one short length of weft at a time.
How it works

Instead of a shuttle carrying a single weft thread across the full width of the cloth, a kani weaver uses kanis — small eyeless wooden bobbins, each wound with a few metres of one colour. A single row of weft might require forty or fifty of them, each inserted for only the span its colour occupies, then handed on.
The talim

The design is not drawn on the loom. It is recorded in a talim: a coded script in which each symbol represents a colour and a number of warp threads. The talim for a full-field shawl can run past four thousand lines. It is read aloud in the workshop, line by line, by a naqash — and it can only be read by someone trained in the notation.
You do not memorise a talim. You listen to it, for two years.
Why it takes so long

A skilled pair working the same loom in shifts might complete a centimetre of finished cloth in a day. A 220 cm shawl is therefore a project measured in seasons, not weeks. Fewer than a hundred full-field kani shawls are completed in Kashmir in a typical year.
How to recognise it

items: Turn it over: on a true kani the reverse shows the pattern in mirror image, with short floating ends where colours change.
Printed imitations have a flat, uniform reverse.
Embroidered pieces sit on top of the ground cloth; kani is the ground cloth.
Look for slight waviness along colour boundaries — evidence of hand tension.

posts.title: Six Ways to Wear a Pashmina Shawl
posts.excerpt: The classic drape, the shoulder fold, the double loop and three more — with notes on which cut suits which.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: A dusty rose cashmere wrap styled over a linen shirt

blocks.text: A shawl is a rectangle of cloth. Everything interesting about wearing one comes from how you fold it before it goes on.
1. The classic drape
Open, centred across the back, both ends falling in front. Formal, and the only way to show off an embroidered border properly. Needs a full 100 cm width to hang correctly.
2. The shoulder fold
Folded once lengthwise, laid over one shoulder, the tail thrown back. The traditional men’s drape, and the easiest to wear over structured tailoring.
3. The double loop
Folded lengthwise into a band, wrapped twice at the neck with the ends tucked. Best with a narrow stole at 70 cm; a full shawl bulks up too much.
4. The belted wrap
Open over the shoulders like a cape, then belted at the waist over a coat. Turns an oversized wrap into outerwear and works particularly well in double-brushed cashmere.
5. The one-shoulder pin
Gathered at one shoulder and held with a brooch. Occasion dressing; leaves the opposite arm free, which matters more than it sounds at a wedding.
6. Simply carried
Folded in four over the forearm. Not a joke — for warm evenings that turn cold, this is what a light Pashmina is actually for.

posts.title: The Best Shawls for Wedding Gifting
posts.excerpt: What to give, what to spend, and why ivory outlasts every other choice. A practical guide to gifting handwoven textiles at Indian weddings.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: A crimson bridal kani shawl presented in a gift box

blocks.text: A shawl is one of the few wedding presents that is still in use twenty years later. It is also one of the easiest to get wrong, because the obvious choices — bright colours, heavy embroidery — are the ones that date fastest.
For the bride

Crimson and deep burgundy are traditional for bridal kani, and a full-field kani shawl is the most significant textile gift that exists in this part of the world. If the budget is not there, an ivory Pashmina with a tilla border does the same job: it reads as ceremonial without competing with the outfit.
For the groom

A plain charcoal or midnight Pashmina shawl, cut to men’s proportions, worn over a bandhgala. Undecorated is the point — it will be worn at every winter wedding for the rest of his life, which an embroidered piece will not.
For the families

Matched sets solve the hardest problem in wedding gifting, which is giving to two people at once without giving them the same thing. A shawl and stole dyed in a single bath read as a pair without being identical.
What to spend

items: Close family: ₹25,000 and above — kani, full sozni, or a numbered piece.
Extended family and close friends: ₹10,000–20,000 — pure Pashmina, tilla border or plain.
Colleagues and wider circle: ₹5,000–10,000 — a boxed Pashmina stole or a fine wool shawl.
Volume gifting: speak to a gifting desk rather than buying retail; most houses box and dispatch individually.

blocks.text: Three rules

items: Choose ivory or a deep neutral when in doubt. It never dates and it suits everyone.
Insist on presentation — the box, the sleeve and the certificate are half the gift.
Include the craft certificate. Knowing who made it is what turns a purchase into an heirloom.

faqs.question: Is it appropriate to gift a shawl at a wedding?
faqs.answer: It is one of the most traditional gifts there is across northern India — shawls have formed part of trousseaus and wedding exchanges for centuries.

faqs.question: What colour should I avoid?
faqs.answer: Avoid white on its own, which carries mourning associations in several communities. Ivory and cream read as celebratory rather than funereal and are the safest neutral choices.

posts.title: A Short History of the Kashmiri Shawl
posts.excerpt: From the Mughal court to Napoleonic Paris to a Scottish mill town that gave the paisley its English name — how a Srinagar textile became a global object.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: An antique jamawar shawl showing a repeating buta motif

blocks.text: The Kashmiri shawl is one of the few Indian textiles that changed European fashion rather than the other way round — and one of the few whose imitation abroad became more famous than the original.
The Mughal century

Shawl weaving in Kashmir is documented from the fifteenth century, but it was under Mughal patronage that it became an industry. Akbar’s court consumed shawls in quantity and standardised the doshala — shawls given in pairs. Jamawar pieces, patterned across the entire ground, were traded along the routes to Kabul and Isfahan and functioned effectively as currency.
The buta becomes the paisley

The teardrop motif that Europe calls paisley is the Kashmiri buta. It arrived in Britain and France around 1800 with shawls carried home by East India Company officers, and demand quickly outran what Srinagar’s looms could supply.

Mills in Norwich, Lyon and — most successfully — Paisley in Renfrewshire began weaving imitations on jacquard looms. The Scottish town produced them in such volume that its name attached itself permanently to a motif that had never been Scottish at all.
Kani and the talim

The technique behind the finest of these shawls is kani: instead of a shuttle carrying one weft across the full width, dozens of small wooden bobbins carry short lengths of coloured yarn, building the pattern thread by thread. A weaver works from a talim — a coded pattern script, read aloud in a workshop by a naqash, that records every colour change in every row.
A full-field kani shawl can take two weavers close to two years. It is still made this way in villages around Kanihama, and the talim is still the only way to record the design.
Collapse and survival

The Franco-Prussian War of 1870 destroyed the French market almost overnight, and European fashion moved on. Kashmir’s shawl economy contracted brutally; thousands of weavers left the trade. What survived did so through domestic Indian demand — trousseau shawls, occasion pieces, and families who kept the looms because the alternative was losing the skill entirely.
The talim outlasts the weaver. That is the point of writing it down.

Today the Kashmir Pashmina GI registration, introduced in 2008, gives the craft a legal identity for the first time — a way of separating hand-processed Changthangi pashm from everything else sold under the name.

posts.title: The Difference Between Pashmina and Wool
posts.excerpt: They are both animal fibres, they both keep you warm, and they behave nothing alike. A practical comparison, by weight, warmth, price and use.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: Pashmina and handloom wool cloth laid side by side for comparison

blocks.text: Both come from animals, both trap air, both are sold as winter cloth. Beyond that they are genuinely different materials, and choosing between them is mostly a question of what you want the piece to do.
Diameter is the whole story
Sheep’s wool used in shawls runs from 19 microns (fine merino) up past 28 (handloom wool). Pashm is 12–15. That single difference produces almost every other difference between the two.
Warmth and weight

Per gram, Pashmina is substantially warmer, because finer fibre packs more insulating air per unit of mass. In absolute terms a heavy 450-gram handloom wool shawl will still out-warm a 180-gram Pashmina one — it simply weighs two and a half times as much and looks it.
Against the skin
Below about 16 microns, wool stops triggering the prickle response. Pashmina and fine cashmere can be worn on bare skin by nearly everyone; ordinary wool cannot.
Durability

Here wool wins. A Kashmiri handloom wool shawl will take daily abuse for decades and improve as it softens. Pashmina wants more care: it pills more readily in its first season, snags on jewellery, and does not enjoy being sat on.
Which to buy

items: For evening, occasion and travel where bulk matters: pure Pashmina.
For daily winter wear, commuting and hard use: fine merino or Kashmiri handloom wool.
For a first serious piece that will be worn constantly: cashmere sits usefully between the two.
For gifting: Pashmina, almost always — it is the piece people keep.

posts.title: How to Care for Your Pashmina
posts.excerpt: Handwoven Pashmina should outlive you. Storing it flat, airing it instead of washing it, and knowing when to call a specialist is most of the job.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: A folded Pashmina shawl resting in a muslin storage sleeve

blocks.text: Fine cashmere is not fragile, but it is unforgiving of the wrong habits. Almost all the damage we see on pieces sent back for repair comes from three things: hangers, washing machines and plastic storage.
Air it, do not wash it

Pashm is naturally antibacterial and does not hold odour the way cotton does. After wearing, hang the piece over a chair back in a ventilated room for a few hours and it will recover on its own. Most shawls need cleaning once a season at most.
When it does need cleaning

items: Embroidered, kani or zari pieces: dry clean only, with someone who handles fine cashmere.
Plain cashmere and merino: hand wash in cold water with a pH-neutral cashmere detergent.
Never wring. Press water out between two towels and dry flat, away from sun and radiators.
Spot-treat marks immediately with a damp cloth and no soap.

blocks.text: Storage

Fold, never hang. A hanger puts the entire weight of the cloth on two points and will distort the shoulders of a shawl within a season. Store folded in the muslin sleeve the piece arrived in, or any breathable cotton bag — plastic traps moisture and invites mildew.

Refold along a different line each year so a permanent crease never sets. Keep a cedar block or a few dried lavender sachets nearby; moths are attracted to protein fibre, and they go for the parts you cannot see.
Pilling and snags

Some pilling in the first season is normal — it is short fibre working its way out, not a fault. Remove it with a cashmere comb, working in one direction, never a razor. If a thread pulls, do not cut it: ease it back through to the reverse with a blunt needle.
What ruins a shawl fastest

items: Perfume sprayed directly onto the cloth — alcohol marks dye permanently.
Jewellery with open settings, which snags a fine weave immediately.
Direct sunlight in storage, which fades natural dyes in months.
Ironing embroidery face-down onto a hard board, which flattens the relief for good.

faqs.question: Can I machine wash a Pashmina shawl?
faqs.answer: No. Even a wool cycle agitates enough to felt fibre this fine. Hand wash plain cashmere in cold water, and dry clean anything embroidered or woven with metallic thread.

faqs.question: How do I get a crease out?
faqs.answer: Hang the piece in a steamy bathroom for twenty minutes, or hold a steamer 20 cm away and let the steam fall through it. Do not press an iron onto embroidery.

faqs.question: How often should I dry clean?
faqs.answer: Once a season at most. Dry cleaning solvents are hard on fine fibre; airing between wears does more good than cleaning does.

posts.title: How to Identify a Quality Pashmina Shawl
posts.excerpt: Six checks you can make in thirty seconds, in any shop, without special equipment — and the two tests that are worth ignoring.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: A cream Pashmina shawl examined closely against natural light

blocks.text: Most buying advice about Pashmina is either mystical or useless. What follows is what an experienced buyer actually does when a shawl is put in front of them.
1. Feel it before you look at it

Genuine pashm registers as warm within a second or two of touching your palm, because it is a poor conductor and immediately traps body heat. Viscose and polyester feel cool and slick. This is the single most reliable field test there is.
2. Hold it to the light

Look at the weave against a window. Hand-spun yarn varies in thickness, so the grid of warp and weft should look slightly irregular — alive rather than printed. A perfectly even, glassy grid means machine yarn.
3. Check the surface for haze
Pashm has a faint halo of fibre ends that gives it a matte, slightly foggy surface. Sheen is a warning sign: silk blends have some lustre by design, but a bright, uniform shine usually means viscose.
4. Look at the edges and fringe

Hand-knotted fringe is uneven in a way that machine overlocking never is. A hand-rolled edge should show tiny irregular stitches on the reverse. Perfect machine hemming on an "artisan" piece is a contradiction worth asking about.
5. Turn the embroidery over

On real sozni work, the reverse is nearly as clean as the face — that is the whole point of the technique, and it is why it takes so long. Loose floats and knots on the back indicate a faster, cheaper stitch.
6. Ask four questions

items: What is the micron grade of the fibre?
Was it hand-spun on a charkha or mill-spun?
Which loom was it woven on, and by whom?
Is there a GI or craft certificate with it?

blocks.text: A serious supplier answers all four without hesitating. A reseller who has never seen the loom will change the subject.
Two tests worth ignoring

The burn test — pulling a thread and lighting it — does distinguish protein fibre from plastic, but it destroys part of the piece and no reputable shop will let you do it. The ring test is charming and often quoted, but it only works on fine unembroidered shawls, and a cheap synthetic scarf passes it easily. Treat it as a demonstration of fineness, not proof of authenticity.

faqs.question: Can I tell quality from price alone?
faqs.answer: Price sets a floor, not a ceiling. Genuine hand-spun, handwoven pure Pashmina below roughly ₹6,000 is implausible on raw material cost alone — but a high price is no guarantee of anything on its own.

faqs.question: What does a GI certificate actually certify?
faqs.answer: The Kashmir Pashmina Geographical Indication mark certifies that the fibre is Changthangi pashm and that the hand-processing took place in Kashmir. It is issued after laboratory fibre testing.

posts.title: What Is Pashmina?
posts.excerpt: Pashmina is a fibre, not a style of shawl. Here is where it comes from, why it costs what it costs, and what the word has come to mean in shops that should know better.
posts.author: Pushmina Editorial

cover.alt: Undyed Pashmina fibre before spinning, photographed in daylight

blocks.text: Ask ten shops what Pashmina is and you will get ten answers, most of them wrong. It is not a weave, a pattern, a size of shawl or a region of manufacture. Pashmina is a fibre — specifically, the winter underfleece of the Changthangi goat.
Where it comes from

Changthangi goats live on the Changthang plateau in Ladakh, at altitudes above 4,000 metres, where winter temperatures fall past −30°C. To survive that, they grow a second coat beneath their outer hair: a dense, extremely fine down called pashm. When spring arrives and the animals begin to moult, herders comb the down out by hand. The goats are never shorn — shearing would cut the coarse outer hair into the fleece and ruin it.
A single goat yields roughly 150 grams of usable fibre a year. A full shawl needs the annual yield of three to four animals. That number, more than anything else, sets the price.
Why fineness matters

Pashm measures between 12 and 15 microns in diameter. Fine merino wool sits around 19 microns; a human hair is closer to 70. Below about 16 microns, wool stops being felt as prickle by almost everyone, which is why Pashmina can be worn directly against the neck by people who find ordinary wool intolerable.

Fineness also explains the warmth-to-weight ratio. A 180-gram Pashmina shawl traps more still air per gram than a 400-gram wool one, so it is warmer than its weight suggests and far less bulky under a coat.
Why it has to be spun by hand

Fibre this fine breaks under the tension of mill spinning. Traditional pashm is spun on a hand charkha, historically almost always by women working at home, at a rate of a few grams an hour. The resulting yarn varies slightly in thickness along its length — and that irregularity is what gives handwoven Pashmina its living surface. Machine-made imitations are perfectly uniform, which is precisely how you spot them.
What the word has come to mean

In much of the market, "pashmina" now describes a size and drape of scarf rather than a material. A great deal of what is sold under the name is viscose, or wool with a token percentage of pashm blended in. Neither is illegal, and neither is necessarily bad cloth — but neither is Pashmina.

items: Genuine pure Pashmina is warm to the touch immediately; viscose feels cool and slippery.
The surface should be matte and faintly hazy, never glossy.
Look closely at the weave: hand-spun yarn is never perfectly even.
Ask for documentation. A real supplier can name the micron grade, the loom and the weaver.

blocks.text: Kashmir’s part in it

The fibre comes from Ladakh; the craft comes from Kashmir. For centuries, raw pashm has travelled to Srinagar to be sorted, dehaired, spun, woven, dyed and embroidered. The Kashmir Pashmina GI registration exists to protect exactly this — the combination of fibre and hand-processing, not the word alone.
Cloth this fine cannot be hurried. Every shortcut shows in the surface.

faqs.question: Is Pashmina the same as cashmere?
faqs.answer: Pashmina is a type of cashmere — the finest grade, from Changthangi goats. All Pashmina is cashmere; most cashmere is not Pashmina. Commercial cashmere is typically 16–19 microns; pashm is 12–15.

faqs.question: Why is pure Pashmina so expensive?
faqs.answer: One goat yields about 150 grams a year and a shawl needs three to four goats’ worth, plus hand-dehairing, hand-spinning and six weeks or more on a handloom. The cost is almost entirely raw fibre and skilled labour.

faqs.question: Does the wedding-ring test prove authenticity?
faqs.answer: Partly. A fine, unembroidered shawl woven from sub-14-micron fibre will pass through a ring, but so will a thin viscose scarf, and a heavier embroidered Pashmina will not. Use it alongside touch, surface and documentation.

landingPages.metaTitle: Pashmina Shawls | Hand-Spun & Handwoven in Kashmir | Pushmina
landingPages.metaDescription: Buy authentic Pashmina shawls hand-spun from Changthangi fibre and handwoven in Kashmir. A buying guide, price expectations and the full Pushmina collection.
intro: A Pashmina shawl is not a category of scarf — it is a shawl woven from pashm, the hand-combed winter underfleece of the Changthangi goat. Everything that distinguishes a good one from a bad one happens before the loom: fibre grade, dehairing, and whether the yarn was spun by hand.
This page explains what to look for and what to expect to pay, then shows every Pashmina shawl we make.

sections.heading: What makes a Pashmina shawl authentic
body: Three things, in order of importance. First, the fibre: genuine pashm measures 12–15 microns, roughly half the diameter of fine merino, and comes from goats wintering above 4,000 metres in Ladakh. Second, the spinning: fibre this fine breaks under mill tension, so it must be spun on a hand charkha. Third, the weave: a wooden handloom, worked slowly enough that the weaver can control tension by feel.
A shawl that fails any of those three is something else — possibly very good cloth, but not Pashmina.

sections.heading: What you should expect to pay
body: One goat yields about 150 grams of usable fibre a year, and a shawl needs the yield of three to four animals plus six weeks or more on a loom. That sets a hard floor on price.
list: Plain pure Pashmina shawl: ₹9,000 – ₹16,000
Ring-test grade, sub-14 micron: ₹15,000 – ₹22,000
Tilla or border embroidery: ₹22,000 – ₹35,000
Full sozni or jamawar: ₹30,000 – ₹50,000
Full-field kani: ₹80,000 and above

sections.heading: Choosing a size
body: A shawl is 100–110 cm wide and 200–220 cm long, and is meant to wrap. A stole is 70 cm or narrower and is meant to hang. If you want to wear the piece open across the back with both ends falling in front, you need the full shawl width — a stole will not drape correctly.
Men’s shawls are cut longer and slightly narrower so they fall in two straight columns from the shoulder.

faqs.question: How can I tell a real Pashmina shawl from a fake?
faqs.answer: Touch it first: genuine pashm feels warm within a second, while viscose feels cool and slippery. Then hold it to the light — hand-spun yarn is slightly irregular, so the weave should look alive rather than perfectly uniform. Finally, ask for the micron grade and the weaver’s name; a real supplier can give you both.

faqs.question: Is Pashmina warmer than wool?
faqs.answer: Per gram, considerably — finer fibre traps more air per unit of mass. A 180 g Pashmina shawl is warmer than a 300 g merino one and far less bulky, though a heavy 450 g handloom wool shawl will still out-warm both in absolute terms.

faqs.question: How should I wash a Pashmina shawl?
faqs.answer: Ideally you should not. Air it after wearing and it will recover on its own. When it does need cleaning, dry clean embroidered pieces and hand wash plain ones in cold water with a pH-neutral cashmere detergent, drying flat away from heat.

landingPages.metaTitle: Kashmiri Shawls | Sozni, Kani & Jamawar Handwork | Pushmina
landingPages.metaDescription: Authentic Kashmiri shawls in sozni embroidery, kani weave, jamawar and tilla work — made in Srinagar by artisan families, with a craft certificate on every piece.
intro: Kashmir’s shawl traditions divide neatly into two families: what is built into the cloth on the loom, and what is added to finished cloth with a needle. Knowing which is which tells you most of what you need about how a shawl was made and what it should cost.

sections.heading: The four crafts
body: Kani is woven: the pattern is constructed thread by thread using dozens of small wooden bobbins, following a coded script called a talim. It is the slowest and rarest of the four.

Sozni is embroidered with a single needle in fine silk thread, worked so precisely that the reverse of the shawl is nearly as clean as the face. Tilla uses flattened metallic thread couched onto the surface, traditionally for occasion and bridal pieces. Jamawar covers the whole ground with woven pattern rather than confining it to a border.

sections.heading: How long each takes
body: Time on the piece is the honest measure of a Kashmiri shawl’s value.
list: Plain handloom shawl: 4–6 weeks on the loom
Border sozni: 3–6 months of needlework
Full sozni: 12–24 months
Jamawar: 3–8 months, depending on colour count
Full-field kani: up to 2 years for two weavers

sections.heading: Buying with confidence
body: Turn every piece over. Real sozni is clean on the reverse; a true kani shows the pattern mirrored with short floating ends where colours change; printed imitations are flat and uniform on the back.
Every Pushmina piece ships with a certificate recording the technique, the fibre grade, the loom and the name of the artisan who finished it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between kani and sozni?
faqs.answer: Kani is a weaving technique — the pattern is built into the cloth on the loom using small wooden bobbins. Sozni is embroidery worked with a needle onto cloth that is already woven. Kani is generally rarer and slower.

faqs.question: Are Kashmiri shawls always Pashmina?
faqs.answer: No. Kashmiri workshops weave Pashmina, fine merino and heavier handloom wool. The craft describes where and how it was made; Pashmina describes the fibre.

faqs.question: What is a talim?
faqs.answer: A coded pattern script used in kani weaving, in which each symbol represents a colour and a number of warp threads. It is read aloud in the workshop and can only be interpreted by someone trained in the notation.

landingPages.metaTitle: Pure Pashmina Shawls | 100% Changthangi Pashm | Pushmina
landingPages.metaDescription: Certified pure Pashmina shawls — nothing blended, nothing substituted. Hand-combed Changthangi fibre, charkha-spun and handwoven in Kashmir.
intro: "Pure" is the word that does the work here. Most cloth sold as pashmina is viscose, or wool carrying a token percentage of pashm. Pure Pashmina means the yarn is entirely Changthangi underfleece, hand-combed rather than shorn, and spun on a charkha rather than a mill frame.

sections.heading: Why blends exist at all
body: Blending is not always dishonest. Adding mulberry silk to the weft has been standard practice in Kashmir for over a century — it produces a lighter, summer-weight cloth with a faint lustre, and it is sold openly as a Pashmina-silk blend.
The problem is blends sold as pure. A 70/30 wool-pashm cloth costs a fraction of pure pashm to produce and is very difficult to distinguish by eye. Documentation is the only real defence.

sections.heading: The ring test, honestly assessed
body: A fine unembroidered shawl woven from sub-14-micron pashm will draw through a wedding ring. It is a genuine demonstration of fineness and it is how buyers have judged cloth in Srinagar’s markets for generations.
It is not proof of authenticity. A thin viscose scarf passes it easily, and a heavier embroidered Pashmina will not pass at all. Use it alongside touch, surface haze and paperwork.

sections.heading: What comes with every piece
body: A craft certificate recording micron grade, loom number and the weaver’s name; an archival muslin sleeve for storage; and a hand-bound presentation box.

faqs.question: What does "pure Pashmina" legally mean?
faqs.answer: Under the Kashmir Pashmina Geographical Indication, the fibre must be Changthangi pashm and the hand-processing must take place in Kashmir. Certification follows laboratory fibre testing.

faqs.question: Is a Pashmina-silk blend inferior?
faqs.answer: Not inferior, different. Silk in the weft gives lighter, more lustrous cloth that knots and drapes well — ideal for scarves and warm-weather layering. It is simply not pure Pashmina, and should never be sold as such.

faqs.question: How long will a pure Pashmina shawl last?
faqs.answer: Decades, with correct care. The pieces that fail early almost always do so through storage mistakes — hangers, plastic bags and direct sunlight — rather than wear.

intro: A shawl is the most useful thing in an Indian wardrobe and the hardest to buy well, because almost every visible feature — colour, pattern, embroidery — is the part that matters least.

sections.heading: Choose by weight, not by look
body: We make women’s shawls in three weights, and the right one depends entirely on use.
list: Pure Pashmina, 170–210 g — evening, occasion and travel, where bulk is the enemy.
Cashmere, 250–320 g — daily winter wear across most of India.
Kashmiri handloom wool, 400 g and above — genuine cold, and the most durable of the three.

sections.heading: Buying your first serious piece
body: Start undyed. An ivory or natural-beige shawl hides nothing: every pick of the weft is visible, so it is the honest way to judge quality, and neutrals outlast every trend.
Save the embroidered and kani pieces for later, when you know how you actually wear a shawl.

sections.heading: Sizes explained
body: A shawl is 100–110 cm wide and 200–220 cm long. A wrap is wider at 120 cm and made to be worn open like a cape. A stole is 70 cm and hangs rather than wraps. If you want to drape a piece open across your back with both ends in front, you need shawl width.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a shawl, a stole and a wrap?
faqs.answer: Width. A stole is around 70 cm and hangs; a shawl is 100–110 cm and wraps; a wrap is 120 cm or more and is worn open like a cape. Length is 200–220 cm in all three.

faqs.question: Which shawl is best for a wedding?
faqs.answer: An ivory Pashmina with a tilla border reads as ceremonial without competing with the outfit, and it will not date. Kani and full sozni pieces are the traditional choice where the budget allows.

faqs.question: How do I stop a shawl from slipping off my shoulders?
faqs.answer: Fold it once lengthwise before draping — the doubled edge grips far better than a single layer — or pin at one shoulder with a brooch for occasion wear.

sections.heading: How to wear one
body: The traditional drape is a single lengthwise fold laid over one shoulder with the tail thrown back — worn over a bandhgala, a kurta or an achkan. Worn open across both shoulders it reads as more formal and needs the full 220 cm length to balance.
Over western tailoring, a narrower stole is usually easier to manage than a full shawl.

sections.heading: Plain or patterned
body: Undecorated wins, almost always. A plain charcoal or midnight Pashmina will be worn at every winter wedding for thirty years; an embroidered piece will be worn twice and then kept for the memory.
If you want one decorated shawl, make it jamawar rather than border embroidery — the pattern reads as texture at conversational distance.

sections.heading: Sizing
body: A 110 × 220 cm shawl suits most men. Below 200 cm the lengthwise fold sits awkwardly on the shoulder; above 230 cm it becomes something to manage rather than wear.

faqs.question: What size should a men’s shawl be?
faqs.answer: 110 × 220 cm suits most men. Anything shorter tends to sit awkwardly once folded lengthwise over the shoulder.

faqs.question: Can a men’s shawl be worn with a suit or overcoat?
faqs.answer: Yes — worn as an oversized scarf, folded lengthwise and left hanging inside the coat. For that use, a 70 cm stole is generally easier than a full shawl.

faqs.question: Pashmina or wool for daily use?
faqs.answer: Wool. Kashmiri handloom wool at 400 g and above takes daily wear for decades and softens as it goes. Keep Pashmina for occasion and travel.

sections.heading: Why a stole is often the better first purchase
body: Stoles cost less than shawls of the same fibre because they use roughly two-thirds of the cloth, and they are far more forgiving to wear: no draping technique required, no bulk at the shoulder, no fuss.

sections.heading: How to wear a stole
body: Folded lengthwise into a band and wrapped twice at the neck is the most useful knot there is. Left long and open over a jacket is the most elegant. Both work at 70 cm; neither works well with a full 110 cm shawl.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a stole and a scarf?
faqs.answer: Length and width. A stole is around 70 × 200 cm; a scarf is narrower at 50 cm and often shorter. A stole can be worn open over the shoulders; a scarf really cannot.

faqs.question: Are Pashmina stoles warm enough for winter?
faqs.answer: For Indian winters and most European autumns, yes. In genuine cold, layer a Pashmina stole under a coat rather than relying on it alone.

body: Every piece is handmade. Dimensions carry a tolerance of ±2 cm, and colour reproduction varies between screens. We describe our pieces as accurately as we can; natural variation in handwoven cloth is inherent to it.

items.question: Is everything you sell handmade?
items.answer: Every piece is hand-finished, and almost everything is handwoven. Our fine merino scarves use mill-spun yarn — we say so on the product page — but they are still finished by hand in our workshop.

items.question: How do I know the Pashmina is genuine?
items.answer: Every Pashmina piece ships with a craft certificate recording the micron grade, the loom and the weaver’s name. Pure Pashmina pieces also carry Kashmir Pashmina GI documentation.

items.question: Why do two pieces of the same design look slightly different?
items.answer: Because they were woven by hand, often by different weavers, and dyed in small batches. Variation is the signature of handwork rather than a defect.

items.question: How long will my order take?
items.answer: Dispatch within 48 hours, then 3–6 working days across India and 7–12 internationally. Express delivery to Indian metro cities is 1–2 days.

items.question: Can I track my order?
items.answer: Yes. A tracking number is emailed and texted at dispatch, and you can enter it on our track order page at any time.

items.question: Do you offer cash on delivery?
items.answer: Yes, on Indian orders up to ₹20,000.

items.question: What is your returns window?
items.answer: 14 days from delivery for unused pieces in their original packaging, with free pickup across India.

items.question: How should I clean a Pashmina shawl?
items.answer: Air it rather than washing it. When it does need cleaning, dry clean embroidered pieces and hand wash plain ones in cold water with a pH-neutral cashmere detergent.

items.question: Do you repair damaged pieces?
items.answer: Yes. Genuine defects are repaired or replaced free within 12 months. Beyond that we repair at cost — send photographs to care@pushmina.com.

items.question: Can you send a gift directly to the recipient?
items.answer: Yes. Add their address and your message at checkout; the parcel goes out with a hand-written card and no pricing inside.

items.question: Do you do corporate gifting?
items.answer: From ten pieces upwards, with optional debossed branding and dispatch to individual addresses. Allow four weeks from artwork approval.
